title: Size-bounded approximate multicommodity-flow sparsifiers
formal: Does there exist a function \(f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\times(0,1)\to\mathbb N\) such that every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G\) with a labelled set \(T\) of \(k\) terminals admits a finite undirected capacitated graph \(H\), containing the same labelled terminals and at most \(f(k,\varepsilon)\) vertices, for which \[\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\le\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\] holds simultaneously for every nonnegative terminal demand vector \(d\)? Here \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and new nonterminal vertices and arbitrary capacities in \(H\) are permitted.
definitions:
A capacitated graph has finitely many vertices, undirected edges and strictly positive finite real capacities \(c_e\). Zero-capacity edges may be deleted and parallel edges combined by summing capacities. The terminals are distinct designated vertices. A demand vector assigns a nonnegative real number \(d_{st}\) to each unordered pair of distinct terminals \(\{s,t\}\).

For each terminal pair, assign nonnegative flow amounts to the finitely many simple paths joining the pair, so that their sum is \(d_{st}\). Commodities may split across paths. The load on an edge is the sum of the assigned amounts over all paths using it, regardless of direction or commodity. The congestion of a routing is \(\max_e \operatorname{load}(e)/c_e\). Define \(\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\) as the infimum over all such routings; set it to infinity if some positive demand cannot be routed. Zero demand has congestion zero, including in an edgeless graph. Inequalities involving infinity use the extended nonnegative reals. Integral, unsplittable and directed flow models are not intended.

Equivalently, let \(P_G\) be the set of demand vectors routable with loads at most the capacities. The requirement is \(P_G\subseteq P_H\subseteq(1+\varepsilon)P_G\), where scalar multiplication multiplies every demand coordinate. This fixes the one-sided normalization of quality. A single \(H\) must work for all demands; choosing a different graph after seeing \(d\) is not allowed.

Size means the number of vertices, including terminals. For simple graphs it also bounds the number of edges quadratically, but no bound on the bit complexity of real capacities is required. The bound is uniform over original graph size, topology and capacity magnitudes. This is an existence question: no efficient construction algorithm or computability requirement on \(f\) is added. The graph \(H\) may be entirely new and need not be a minor, quotient, contraction or subgraph of \(G\). Exact preservation corresponds to zero error and is outside the stated positive-error domain.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must provide fixed \(k\) and fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) for which no finite vertex bound works for all input graphs. Exact-sparsifier lower bounds alone, or lower bounds restricted to contraction-based sparsifiers, do not refute this statement. A positive answer must produce a graph realizing the simultaneous routing inequalities; a non-graph encoding of feasible demands does not suffice.
context:
Andoni, Gupta and Krauthgamer obtain bounded-size near-exact flow sparsifiers for quasi-bipartite graphs and a more general compact sketch. Their general graph-representation question distinguishes a graph from an abstract encoding of its routing behavior.

Krauthgamer and Mosenzon show that exact flow preservation can require unbounded size even with six terminals. Positive approximation error is essential to the retained question.

Chen and Tan prove a six-terminal obstruction to bounded-size near-exact contraction-based sparsifiers. They explicitly restrict this negative result to contraction constructions; it is not an impossibility theorem for every graph H allowed here.

The 2026 lower bounds also concern contraction-based sparsifiers, including extensions discussed in the paper. Their extra hypotheses must not be dropped when assessing the unrestricted question.
why: This tests whether terminal flow behavior admits an arbitrarily accurate finite summary independent of the original network.

progress.text: Near-exact graph sparsifiers are obtained for quasi-bipartite inputs, together with general compact flow sketches.
Unbounded size is proved necessary for exact flow sparsifiers with six terminals.
The corresponding positive-error obstruction is established for contraction-based sparsifiers.
Further size-quality lower bounds are given for contraction-based sparsifiers with Steiner vertices.

import_provenance.original_statement: For every undirected capacitated graph with k terminals and every ε>0, does there exist a graph of size f(k,ε), independent of the original graph’s size and capacities, preserving all terminal multicommodity-flow congestion values within 1+ε? The sparsifier may have new nonterminal vertices and need not be obtained by contraction.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: Exact preservation is already impossible with size bounded solely by k, even for six terminals. The contraction-only (1+ε) version also has six-terminal obstructions; neither settles unrestricted approximate graph sparsifiers.

sentences: A network has a small distinguished set of terminal vertices and may have many internal vertices.
The question asks whether another graph of size depending only on terminal count and positive error can preserve every fractional terminal routing.
The replacement graph may use new vertices and need not arise by contraction.
Known exact and contraction-based impossibility results have restrictions absent from this question.
A positive result would separate the complexity of a network interface from the size and capacity range of its interior.
